506	Let us mention in this context an idea that is simple,
507	wonderful, sublime, an idea that fills the heart with strength,
508	that truly gives something to hold on to in these last moments
509	of the exile.
510	The custom of the Sephardim, the custom of the Eastern communities,
511	is to begin the Kinot on the night of Tisha beAv with the Kinah
512	of Haazinu.
513	Even before the other Kinot, they begin
514	to read the Kinah of Haazinu, the terrible prophecies of destruction
515	that Moshe Rabbeinu said. The Kinah of Haazinu foretells
516	bad days, hard days, that even the greatest prophets of destruction
517	did not foresee like them. Moshe Rabbeinu says verses
518	that are hard even to repeat. He quotes
519	the Holy One, blessed be He: I said, days will come when the Holy One,
520	blessed be He, will say, "I said I would scatter them to the corners,
521	I will cast them out like the corner of the field. I will throw the people of
522	Israel to the corners of the world, one Jew here, one Jew
523	there, so that they lose all meaning. Grain
524	that is gathered together, that is collected, has importance, has
525	weight, has volume, has meaning. But

529	weight. I will cast the people of Israel

532	"I will make their memory cease from mankind."
533	Days will come when the Holy One, blessed be He, will want to wipe out

549	Let us picture terrible and dreadful things. There are no other
550	harsh and terrible prophecies like the Kinah of
551	Haazinu. And here one question arises: so why is it a song?
552	Why is Haazinu a song and not a lament on the night of Tisha beAv?
553	The Eastern communities read it as a Kinah,
554	but all year round it is a song. First, in the Torah itself it
555	is written in rhyme. Second, it is written like two
556	columns with a break in the middle, the way a song is written. Third,
557	in the Beit HaMikdash the Levites would sing it, truly
558	with song and melody. Every Shabbat they would sing "Haziv Lakh."
559	"Haziv Lakh" means they would divide the song of Haazinu
560	into six parts, and each Shabbat they would sing one part.
561	Accordingly, in the synagogue we divide
562	the first part of Haazinu into six aliyot. "Hazinu Haazinu,"
563	"Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak," "the days of old," we divide the song of Haazinu into six
564	parts
565	and read the first six aliyot the way
566	the Levites would sing in the Beit HaMikdash. They sing for six Shabbatot
567	and then start over again. How can we
568	imagine what the Levites sang? "I said I would scatter them,"
569	in what melody did they sing this? We are speaking
570	of terrible prophecies of exile, which must be read
571	sitting on the ground on the night of Tisha beAv,
572	and the Levites would sing suffering, sing pain. An enormous question:
573	what lies here, is Haazinu a song, or is Haazinu
574	a Kinah? How can we understand the whole matter?
575	The Rebbe once said a truly brilliant thing in Likutei Sichot,
576	in a short note he said it, but it is truly so special:
577	Haazinu is a song
578	because it films the whole path.
579	Haazinu is a song because it is a panoramic picture
580	of all the chapters, of all the stages of the life of the people of
581	Israel. Haazinu, says the Ramban, portrays past, present,
582	and future. In the song of Haazinu, the suffering, the pain, the
583	terrible lament is a chapter
584	within the great plan that leads to the Redemption.
585	And over this a Jew sings, not over this moment, but over the understanding
586	that this moment creates redemption, creates good,
587	creates a greatness that the good days did not create.
588	A Jew does not sing over this moment as it is, but over
589	this moment as part of the movement of the train, part
590	of the progress of the ship,
591	of the progress of the route, part of the trouble
592	that turns into a skylight and builds the future Redemption. Let us
593	see. Here He began with the past: "He found him in a desert land,"

596	the Holy One, blessed be He, carried us like an eagle on
597	its wings, we were at the peak of the world, at the summit of the world.
598	And then we come to the present, we come to the terrible exile.
